[[File:Onominato Shrine Ujikofuda dark reverse.jpg|thumb|An Ujikofuda from {{ill|Onominato Shrine|ja|大野湊神社}}]] 
{{Short description|Japanese historical law}}

The {{Nihongo|'''Shrine Parishioner Registration act'''|氏子調|Ujiko shirabe}} was a law in Japan that forcibly registered people in Shinto Shrines.<ref name="inoue-2023a">{{Cite web |last=Inoue |first=Nobutaka |title=Shrine Parishioner Registration (ujiko shirabe) |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8871 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230312235441/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=8871 |archive-date=12 Mar 2023 |access-date=12 Mar 2023 |website=[[Kokugakuin University]] Encyclopedia of Shinto}}</ref><ref name="berthon-1995a">{{Cite journal |last=Berthon |first=Jean-Pierre |date=April 1995 |title=Helen Hardacre, Shinto and the State, 1868-1988, Princeton, NJ, Princeton University Press, « Studies in Church and State », 1989, XVI-203 p. |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/s0395264900054135 |journal=Annales. Histoire, Sciences Sociales |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=28–29 |doi=10.1017/s0395264900054135 |s2cid=165716719 |issn=0395-2649|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It was implemented by the [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji government]] from 1871 (Meiji 4) to 1873.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Thal |first=Sarah |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4bQbNeJJ_ogC&dq=ujiko+shirabe&pg=PA184 |title=Rearranging the Landscape of the Gods: The Politics of a Pilgrimage Site in Japan, 1573-1912 |date=February 2005 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-79421-1 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Jaffe |first=Richard M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s1MgEAAAQBAJ&dq=ujiko+shirabe&pg=PT100 |title=Neither Monk nor Layman: Clerical Marriage in Modern Japanese Buddhism |date=2021-06-08 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-23109-9 |language=en}}</ref> It is a religious policy that obliged citizens to become [[Ujigami|parishioners of local]] [[Shinto shrine|shrines]] (gosha).<ref name="inoue-2023a" /><ref name="berthon-1995a" />

Previously the status of [[ujiko]] was limited to privileged local families, but this system extended it to everyone in the village.<ref name="berthon-1995a" />

The official name of the law is {{nihongo|[[Daijō-kan]] Proclamation No. 322 "Investigation of parishioners at large and small shrines"|太政官布告第三二二号「大小神社氏子取調」|Daijōkanfukoku dai san ni ni-gō `daishō jinja ujiko torishirabe'}}'''.'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Beckmann |first=George M. |date=1954 |title=Political Crises and the Crystallization of Japanese Constitutional Thought, 1871-1881 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3635567 |journal=Pacific Historical Review |volume=23 |issue=3 |pages=259–270 |doi=10.2307/3635567 |jstor=3635567 |issn=0030-8684|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Overview ==
{{Commons category|Ujikofuda}}
The law had seven parts. The first part said that when a baby was born, the parents had to tell the village head. Then, they had to take the baby to the local shrine to get a special {{Nihongo|Amulet|氏子札|Ujikofuda}}. This amulet had to stay with the baby. If someone did not have this amulet, they had to tell the village head their name, birthdate, where they were born, and their father's name. The village head would then get an amulet for them. The village head would check the amulets every six years when they did a registration exercise. If someone died, their amulet had to go back to the shrine priest.<ref name="inoue-2023a" /> 

The law also required all households to hold [[Jingū taima]] and as such all households were branch shrines of [[Ise Jingu]].<ref name="berthon-1995a" />

This meant each household had the "divided spirit" of the Ise deities. Before, households had a simple purification talisman. Shrine registration aimed to unite the nation under the worship of Ise deities.<ref name="berthon-1995a" /> But, it wasn't successful as a census system. Shrines still made local residents their parishioners. This practice increased the support for shrines. It also expanded the idea of shrine affiliation based on where one lived.<ref name="berthon-1995a" /> Talismans continued to be placed in household altars. Before the Meiji era, only a few families were considered shrine parishioners. Now, shrines claimed anyone in their area as a parishioner. These changes in shrine membership became more evident in the twentieth century.<ref name="berthon-1995a" />

Another set of rules was made at the same time called Regulations for Rural District Shrines. This set of rules said that each district had to have one rural district shrine responsible for overseeing registration. These rules were supposed to register all newborn babies. Some people think that these rules were also supposed to replicate the [[Danka system]] which did a similar thing with Buddhist temples. These rules only lasted for two years, but the rules for district shrines lasted until after [[World War II]].<ref name="inoue-2023a" /> The [[Shrine Consolidation Policy]] merged shrines together for this purpose.<ref name="kokugakuin">{{Cite web |date=2011-05-20 |title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home : Modern and Contemporary : Jinja gōshi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1105 |access-date=2023-04-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110520011051/http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1105 |archive-date=2011-05-20 }}</ref>
